title: How do novice runners with different body mass indexes begin a self-chosen running regime?
authors: Bertelsen ML, Hansen M, Rasmussen S, Nielsen RO
journal: Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy
population: Novice runners with GPS watches, first week of a self-chosen regime: 405 normal weight, 341 overweight, 168 obese
findings: Exploratory 7-day prospective cohort with GPS watch data on distance, duration, speed and date of each session (n=914).

In session 1, overweight runners ran 0.5 km/h slower (95% CI -0.8 to -0.2) and obese runners 1.7 km/h slower (95% CI -2.0 to -1.4) than normal weight; obese runners also ran 0.4 km less (95% CI -0.7 to -0.2).
Over the first week, overweight (-0.5 km/h) and obese runners (-1.7 km/h) ran slower than normal weight runners, while running distance and duration were similar.
Authors: overweight and obese runners selected a similar training dose to normal-weight runners, which may partly explain their higher injury risk seen in other studies.
limitations: Descriptive, 7 days only, volunteers with GPS watches; no injury outcome in this paper.
implications: Heavier novices self-select about the same first-week dose as lighter runners, so the plan (not the runner) has to scale the starting dose by BMI.
Inference, not a finding: because heavier runners run slower, prescribing the floor week by time at an easy pace rather than by distance may suit them.
